why: A subset's OR is at most k iff its OR equals some mask m <= k, i.e. every chosen value is a submask of m. So for each m <= k take every positive-profit item whose value is a submask of m; summing those gains over all submasks is a sum-over-subsets (SOS) DP on the 10-bit masks.
hints: OR only ever turns bits on. If the final OR is some mask m, what must be true of each chosen value?
Each chosen value must be a submask of m. So for a fixed m, take every item with value submask of m and positive profit; the answer is the best m <= k.

gain[v] = total positive profit at value v; run SOS DP (for each bit, best[m] += best[m ^ bit] when the bit is set) to get best[m] for all 1024 masks; answer max(best[m] for m <= k), at least 0. O(n + 10 * 1024).
pitfalls: 'OR at most k' compares numbers, not bit sets: with k = 4, an OR of 3 is allowed though 3 is not a submask of 4. Enumerate every mask m <= k, not just submasks of k.
Never take negative-profit items; the empty subset gives 0.
Duplicate values must sum their profits, not overwrite.
